subject: Science
title: Meera's Sky Adventure
hook: Explore the air we breathe, water we drink, and weather above us!

slides.title: Air, Water, Weather
slides.storyContext: Meera discovers the invisible air, precious water, and changing weather around her village.

image.alt: Air, Water, Weather — Air, Water, Weather

slides.title: Meera's Flying Kite
slides.storyContext: Meera flies a kite on a windy day. She can't see the wind, but she feels it push her kite. 'What IS this wind?' she wonders. Teacher Singh smiles. 'That's air moving. Let me show you how air works and shapes our weather.'

slides.title: What is Air?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh fills a balloon with air. 'Air is all around us, but we can't see it. Yet it's real!'

points.label: Air is invisible
points.text: You can't see air, but it fills every space around us.

points.label: We breathe air
points.text: Inside air is oxygen—we breathe it in to live.

points.label: Air has weight
points.text: Air pushes in all directions. This push is called air pressure.

points.label: Air moves
points.text: Moving air is wind. It can push things like kites, boats, and leaves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Air is an invisible gas all around us that we breathe and that makes wind.

slides.title: Water - Life's Liquid
slides.storyContext: Meera and Teacher Singh walk to the well to get drinking water.

points.label: Where is water?
points.text: Water is in lakes, rivers, wells, oceans, and clouds.

points.label: We need water
points.text: All living things—people, plants, animals—need water to survive.

points.label: Water covers Earth
points.text: Oceans, rivers, and lakes cover most of Earth's surface.

points.label: Water changes form
points.text: Water can be liquid (rivers), solid (ice), or gas (steam and clouds).

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is the precious liquid that all life on Earth needs.

slides.title: Weather - Air on the Move
slides.storyContext: Dark clouds gather in the sky. Teacher Singh points up. 'Weather is what the air and sky are doing right now.'

points.label: What is weather?
points.text: Weather is the condition of air and sky at any moment—sunny, rainy, windy, hot, cold.

points.label: Weather changes
points.text: Air temperature, wind, clouds, and rain change throughout the day and seasons.

points.label: We observe weather
points.text: We see clouds, feel wind, measure temperature, and watch for rain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weather is what we see and feel in the sky and air each day.

slides.title: Rain - Water Falling from Clouds
slides.storyContext: Rain begins to fall. 'Where does rain come from?' Meera asks. Teacher Singh explains the water cycle.

points.label: How does rain form?
points.text: Water from oceans and rivers rises as invisible vapor. It cools in the sky and forms clouds.

points.label: Clouds hold droplets
points.text: Tiny water droplets cluster together in clouds, getting heavier.

points.label: Rain falls
points.text: When droplets are too heavy, they fall as rain back to Earth.

points.label: Cycle repeats
points.text: Rain feeds rivers and oceans, then evaporates again—the water cycle goes on.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rain is water from oceans and rivers falling from clouds in the sky.

image.alt: Rain - Water Falling from Clouds — Air, Water, Weather

slides.title: Wind - Moving Air
slides.storyContext: The wind grows stronger. Meera's dupatta flutters. Teacher Singh says wind is air that moves.

points.label: What causes wind?
points.text: When air heats or cools unevenly, it moves from one place to another.

points.label: Wind has power
points.text: Strong wind can move leaves, dust, water, and even fly kites and sailing boats.

points.label: Different speeds
points.text: A breeze is gentle. A storm wind is fast and powerful.

points.label: We use wind
points.text: Windmills use wind to pump water. Sails use wind to move boats.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wind is air that moves because of heat differences. It can push and carry things.

slides.title: A Day of Weather
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh describes what happens on a typical monsoon day in the village.

example.problem: In the morning, it's hot and still. By noon, dark clouds arrive. By afternoon, strong wind blows and heavy rain falls. Water flows in streams. By evening, wind stops and sun appears. Explain what is happening to air, water, and weather.
example.solution: Morning: still, warm air and high temperature. Noon: water vapor rises from fields and rivers, cools high in sky, forms clouds. Afternoon: pressure difference causes wind to blow; condensed water falls as rain. Wind carries the rain over the land. Evening: storm passes, air cools, wind stops, water drains away, sun breaks through clouds.

image.alt: A Day of Weather — Air, Water, Weather

slides.title: Guess the Weather
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh gives Meera clues to guess what weather is coming.

example.problem: Dark clouds are gathering. The wind is blowing hard. The air feels cool and damp. What weather is coming? And what should Meera do to stay safe?
example.solution: Rain and possibly a storm are coming. Meera should: bring the kite indoors, move away from trees, go inside the house, close windows and doors, stay inside until the storm passes.

slides.title: What Meera Learned
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets and the rain stops, Meera watches a rainbow. She feels the light breeze.

points.text: Air is invisible but real. We breathe it, and it creates wind.
Water is found in oceans, rivers, lakes, wells, clouds, and rain.
Weather is what the air and sky do: sunny, rainy, windy, hot, or cold.
Rain comes from the water cycle: water rises, forms clouds, falls as rain.
Wind is air that moves and can push things across Earth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Air, water, and weather are always changing and shaping the world around us.

image.alt: What Meera Learned — Air, Water, Weather

subject: Science
title: Arun's Market Discovery
hook: Learn about materials we use every day—and what they're made of!

slides.title: Materials Around Us
slides.storyContext: Arun visits the market and discovers that everything is made of different materials.

image.alt: Materials Around Us — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Exploring the Market
slides.storyContext: Arun's mother takes him to the market. He sees clothes, pots, toys, and food everywhere. His sister picks up a wooden toy, then a metal spoon. 'Why is this one hard and this one softer?' she asks. Shopkeeper Uncle smiles. 'Because they are made of different materials! Let me show you.'

image.alt: Exploring the Market — Materials Around Us

slides.title: What is a Material?
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle gathers different objects—a clay pot, a steel knife, a cloth bag, and a wooden box.

points.label: Material means
points.text: The 'stuff' something is made from. Like clay, steel, cloth, wood, plastic.

points.label: Everything has a material
points.text: Your shirt is cloth. A pot is clay or metal. A toy is plastic or wood.

points.label: Materials have properties
points.text: Some are hard. Some are soft. Some are bendy. Some are shiny. Each material is different.

slides.inSimpleWords: A material is what something is made of. Different materials feel and look different.

image.alt: What is a Material? — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Natural Materials - From Nature
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle shows Arun things that come directly from nature.

points.label: Wood from trees
points.text: Chairs, boxes, and sticks are made from wood. It's strong, can be carved, and burns.

points.label: Clay from earth
points.text: Pots, bricks, and dishes are made by digging clay from the ground and shaping it.

points.label: Wool from sheep
points.text: Sweaters and blankets are made from sheep's wool. It's warm and soft.

points.label: Cotton from plants
points.text: Clothes and bags are made from cotton. It grows in fields, is soft, and breathes well.

slides.inSimpleWords: Natural materials come directly from nature—like wood, clay, wool, and cotton.

slides.title: Metals - Strong and Shiny
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle pulls out a steel spoon, a brass bell, and an aluminum pot.

points.label: What are metals?
points.text: Hard, shiny materials dug from under Earth. Iron, steel, copper, brass, aluminum.

points.label: Properties of metal
points.text: They are hard, shiny, conduct heat and electricity, and can be bent.

points.label: How we use metals
points.text: Spoons, pots, pans, bells, coins, jewelry, tools, cars.

slides.inSimpleWords: Metals are hard, shiny materials we dig from Earth and use for tools and dishes.

image.alt: Metals - Strong and Shiny — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Plastic - A Human-Made Material
slides.storyContext: Arun's sister grabs a plastic water bottle and a toy car. 'These don't come from nature,' Shopkeeper Uncle says.

points.label: What is plastic?
points.text: Plastic is made by humans from oil. It's light, strong, and doesn't break easily.

points.label: Why use plastic?
points.text: It's cheap, water-proof, and we can mold it into any shape—bottles, toys, bags, buckets.

points.label: A problem
points.text: Plastic doesn't rot away. It stays in Earth for hundreds of years. We should reuse it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plastic is made by humans and can be shaped into anything. But it takes forever to break down.

slides.title: Glass - Clear and Hard
slides.storyContext: A glass window in the shop catches sunlight. Shopkeeper Uncle taps it gently.

points.label: What is glass?
points.text: Glass is made by heating sand at very high temperatures.

points.label: Properties of glass
points.text: It's hard, clear, smooth, and you can see through it.

points.label: How we use it
points.text: Windows, drinking glasses, mirrors, jars, light bulbs.

points.label: Careful—
points.text: Glass is fragile and breaks easily into sharp pieces. Handle with care.

slides.inSimpleWords: Glass is made from sand and is clear, hard, and smooth—but breaks easily.

slides.title: A Day in Materials
slides.storyContext: Arun's mother asks him to describe everything he used from morning to evening.

example.problem: From morning to evening, Arun uses many things: his cotton shirt, wooden school desk, steel spoon at breakfast, clay pot for water, plastic water bottle, glass window, metal door handle, and a wooden toy. Name the material each is made from and why it works well for that job.
example.solution: Cotton shirt: natural, soft, breathes well. Wooden desk: natural, strong, sturdy. Steel spoon: metal, hard, conducts heat, doesn't rust. Clay pot: natural, holds water, cool. Plastic bottle: human-made, light, water-proof. Glass window: clear, lets light in, hard. Metal handle: conducts heat, strong, durable. Wooden toy: natural, can be carved, warm to touch.

image.alt: A Day in Materials — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Match the Material to the Job
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle plays a matching game with Arun.

example.problem: Match each job to the best material: 1) Making a raincoat. 2) Making a cooking pot. 3) Making a toy block. 4) Making a door handle. Options: Wood, metal, plastic, clay.
example.solution: 1) Raincoat = plastic (water-proof). 2) Cooking pot = metal (conducts heat well). 3) Toy block = wood (safe, warm to touch, can be carved). 4) Door handle = metal (strong and durable).

slides.title: Arun's Discovery
slides.storyContext: As they leave the market, Arun sees materials everywhere and understands what each is made of.

points.text: Materials are the stuff things are made from: wood, clay, metal, wool, cotton, plastic, glass.
Natural materials come from nature: wood, clay, wool, cotton, silk.
Metal materials are hard, shiny, strong, and conduct heat.
Plastic is made by humans and is light, water-proof, and can be shaped.
Glass is made from sand and is clear, hard, but breaks easily.

slides.inSimpleWords: Everything around us is made of a material. Different materials have different properties and uses.

subject: Science
title: Kabir's Sky School
hook: Learn about Earth, the Sun, day and night, and seasons!

slides.title: The Earth and Sun
slides.storyContext: Kabir and Ajay learn why we have day and night, and why seasons change throughout the year.

slides.title: Why Does the Sun Disappear?
slides.storyContext: Kabir and Ajay sit on the rooftop watching the sunset. 'Where does the sun go at night?' Ajay asks. 'Will it come back tomorrow?' Teacher Lata joins them with a flashlight and globe. 'Let me show you how Earth and Sun move together.'

image.alt: Why Does the Sun Disappear? — The Earth and Sun

slides.title: What is the Sun?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata shines the flashlight bright. 'This is like the Sun. A huge, hot star in the sky.'

points.label: The Sun is huge
points.text: It's a giant ball of hot, glowing gas that floats in space.

points.label: It gives light and heat
points.text: Light from the Sun reaches Earth, giving us day, warmth, and energy.

points.label: It's far away
points.text: The Sun is so far that light takes 8 minutes to reach us.

points.label: It never moves
points.text: The Sun stays in place. Earth moves around the Sun.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Sun is a giant, hot, glowing star that gives Earth light and heat.

slides.title: What is Earth?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata spins the globe slowly. 'This is Earth—and we live on it!'

points.label: Earth is round
points.text: Earth is a sphere—like a giant ball floating in space.

points.label: It rotates
points.text: Earth spins like a top, turning once every 24 hours.

points.label: It orbits the Sun
points.text: Earth moves around the Sun in a circle, taking 365 days (one year).

points.label: We're on the surface
points.text: We live on Earth's outer surface. Gravity holds us down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is a round planet that spins once a day and circles the Sun once a year.

image.alt: What is Earth? — The Earth and Sun

slides.title: Day and Night - Earth Spinning
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata dims the lights and spins the globe while shining the flashlight on one side.

points.label: Why day and night?
points.text: As Earth spins, different parts face the Sun at different times.

points.label: Day side
points.text: The part facing the Sun gets light and warmth. That's daytime there.

points.label: Night side
points.text: The opposite side faces away and is in darkness. That's nighttime.

points.label: Rotation takes time
points.text: Earth takes 24 hours (one day) to spin once. That's why we have day and night.

slides.inSimpleWords: Day and night happen because Earth spins. Your side faces the Sun = day. Your side faces away = night.

slides.title: Seasons - Earth's Tilted Path
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata shows how Earth tilts as it goes around the Sun. 'This tilt creates seasons!'

points.label: Earth is tilted
points.text: Earth doesn't stand straight. It tilts at an angle of 23.5 degrees.

points.label: Summer and Winter
points.text: When your part tilts toward the Sun = summer (hot, long days). When it tilts away = winter (cold, short days).

points.label: Spring and Fall
points.text: As Earth orbits, the tilt changes: spring and fall are in-between seasons.

points.label: Cycle repeats
points.text: After 365 days, Earth completes one orbit and the cycle repeats. Seasons happen again.

slides.inSimpleWords: Seasons change because Earth is tilted and orbits the Sun. Tilt toward Sun = summer. Tilt away = winter.

slides.title: Shadows and Sunlight
slides.storyContext: Kabir notices his shadow is long in the morning and short at noon. Teacher Lata explains.

points.label: Shadows change with time
points.text: As the Sun moves across the sky, shadows change direction and length.

points.label: Morning shadows
points.text: Sun is low on horizon = long shadow pointing away from Sun.

points.label: Noon shadows
points.text: Sun is high overhead = shadow is short and below the object.

points.label: Evening shadows
points.text: Sun is low again = long shadow pointing the opposite way.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shadows move and change size as the Sun moves across the sky during the day.

image.alt: Shadows and Sunlight — The Earth and Sun

slides.title: A Full Year's Journey
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata describes what happens to Earth over one complete year.

example.problem: Explain what happens to Kabir's village over one year: the length of days, temperature, and shadows as Earth orbits the Sun. Describe spring, summer, fall, and winter.
example.solution: Spring: Days get longer, temperature rises, shadows shorten at noon. Summer: Days are longest, very hot, noon shadows shortest. Fall: Days get shorter, temperature drops, shadows lengthen. Winter: Days are shortest, very cold, noon shadows longest. Then the cycle repeats. This happens because Earth's tilt makes different seasons as it orbits the Sun.

slides.title: Predict the Time
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata points to different shadows and asks Kabir to guess the time of day.

example.problem: Look at shadows. Shadow 1 is very long pointing west. Shadow 2 is very short under the object. Shadow 3 is long pointing east. When in the day do these shadows happen?
example.solution: Shadow 1 (long, pointing west) = morning (Sun in the east). Shadow 2 (short) = noon (Sun high overhead). Shadow 3 (long, pointing east) = evening (Sun in the west).

slides.title: Kabir's Cosmic Understanding
slides.storyContext: As stars appear in the night sky, Kabir feels connected to the cosmos.

points.text: The Sun is a giant hot star giving Earth light and heat.
Earth is a round planet that spins once per day (rotation).
Earth's rotation causes day and night.
Earth orbits the Sun once per year. The tilt causes seasons.
Shadows tell us the Sun's position in the sky and help us tell time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth spins to make day and night. Earth orbits to make seasons. The Sun powers it all.
